https://aa.com.tr/en/eurasia/ukraine-nor.text: Europe Eurasia Ukraine, Norway sign defense cooperation, strategic partnership agreements Zelenskyy says agreements strengthen defense, energy, resilience partnership between two countries Kanyshai Butun 23 August 2026 • Update : 23 August 2026 İSTANBUL Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store signed defense cooperation and strategic partnership agreements on Sunday. Zelenskyy said the agreements strengthen the foundation of the two countries’ long-term partnership in defense, energy and resilience. He thanked Norway for maintaining a high level of support and pledging about $9 billion in aid for Ukraine in 2027. “Together with Prime Minister of Norway Jonas Gahr Store, we signed an Agreement on defence and security cooperation under the Drone Deal format and a Declaration on a Strategic Partnership – the Ellisiv Accord, named after the daughter of Prince Yaroslav the Wise, who became Queen of Norway,” Zelenskyy wrote on US social media platform X. Store earlier announced that Norway will provide Ukraine with 85 billion kroner ($9.2 billion) in new aid in 2027, including 70 billion kroner ($7.5 billion) for military support and 15 billion kroner ($1.6 billion) for civilian assistance. The 2027 commitment will mark the third consecutive year Norway has provided 85 billion kroner in annual support to Ukraine. Store arrived in Kyiv on Sunday to attend a Nordic-Baltic Eight summit hosted by Zelenskyy. The summit was also attended by Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs, Finnish President Alexander Stubb, Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal and Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda. news_share news_share_description subscription_contact subscription LATEST NEWS All US restricts official travel to Mexican border city of Nogales, citing threat Netanyahu’s Likud slips further as path to governing majority narrows: Poll AfD hails 'historic' Saxony-Anhalt election victory AfD election victory in Germany dominates international headlines Cargo plane overruns runway at Miami airport, prompting ground stop Türkiye retain European women's volleyball title with 3-2 win over Italy Netanyahu vows to strike Iran as popularity declines 50 days before elections See All Zelenskyy denies Ukraine’s involvement in Nord Stream 2 blasts UK’s Burnham to visit Kyiv on 1st foreign trip as prime minister

Is there life after drugs? As serious as drug addiction may be, treatment, willpower and adequate help can lead to abstinence and help build a stable and fulfilling life. Photo: pixabay.com@MrWashingt0n Roxana Vasile , 09.09.2026, 13:00 The European Commissioner for internal affairs and migration Magnus Brunner and the European Union Drugs Agency (EUDA) presented the 2026 European Drug Report in the first half of June. Based on data from 29 countries (27 EU member states plus Norway and Turkey) the document shows that as they have become more available, more diverse and more potent, drugs have an increasingly negative impact on the health of consumers. At the same time, drug trafficking is a major threat to security on the continent. Organised crime networks are diversifying trafficking routes and methods of evading controls, using intimidation and violence, and recruiting and exploiting vulnerable young people. The anti-drug expert Cătălin Țone gave Radio Romania more details about the European Report: Cătălin Țone: “There is data that raises concern, in my opinion. Basically, the document officially announces that a new drug appears in Europe almost every week. Increasingly powerful drugs, which are increasingly difficult to monitor, are flooding the market. The diversity of substances is great and the possibility of them causing serious effects exists almost at every step. The report also warns against synthetic opioids as the main cause for concern, because they are very concentrated: thousands of lethal doses can be made from a single gram of certain substances.” Georgiana Drăgan was addicted to drugs for eight years. Georgiana Drăgan: “At 17 I started using marijuana occasionally, for three years. Then, unfortunately, after I went into a relationship with a boy addicted to heroin, I started using this drug and a severe heroin addiction followed, which lasted five years. It had consequences on all aspects of my life, from undermining all the relationships I had, to the inability to keep a job, to various offences, including thefts, robberies, loans against fictitious documents, etc. But the most painful were the problems I caused my family, especially my mother, and the state of helplessness I had reached.” In 2009, when she realised that she was no longer in control and that she had to stop, Georgiana joined a rehab programme: Georgiana Drăgan: “The lowest point and what led me to make the decision was the fact that I had lost everything. From a girl with aspirations for the future, a girl with potential, an award-winning athlete, an Olympian at school, I had ended up sleeping on cardboard boxes in the stairwell of an apartment building and having absolutely nothing to fight for. That was the moment when I realised that if I didn’t make a change, I would end up in prison or in the grave. And somehow this realisation made me think about myself, the person I had been in the past, the child and teenager with dreams and aspirations, and I finally made a decision. But the decision wouldn’t have been enough if I hadn’t had a place to recover, because I had wanted to quit before, but the fact that there was something concrete to help me this time around made all the difference.” Not only did Georgiana Drăgan quit drugs, but she became the director of the Teen Challenge centre for girls, near Bucharest. Nine girls are currently enrolled in the rehab and social integration programme, which lasts between 9 months and a year for adults. And the approach is holistic: Georgiana Drăgan: “We recommend a detox period before joining our program, because these people need to be helped to cope with the symptoms of withdrawal. But beyond that, an approach is needed in which they are helped to rebuild their lives from scratch, and this is done by establishing new life principles, by changing values. People who lied, manipulated, who were used to making a combination to get money, should now have healthy principles that will help not only during the recovery period, but also afterwards. Our schedule is well structured, starting from the time we wake up until the time we go to bed, there are diverse activities throughout the day, so that neither boredom nor overload or fatigue occurs. We have a mentoring system, a form of counselling, we have courses, so we also address this educational part and, very importantly, our programme addresses one’s deepest side, because each of us has their own inner universe, their own identity… So the first phase is the recovery phase, and then there is an internship period in which responsibilities increase, privileges also increase, they get a phone, they have interaction with the outside world. They also have the opportunity to help other people in their turn, thus becoming role models and giving hope.” The success rate, says the director of the Teen Challenge centre Georgiana Drăgan, is very high. Many of those who chose to follow this program have finished it. This shows that, no matter how serious the drug addiction is, through specialised treatment, willpower and adequate help, addicted people can achieve abstinence and build a stable and fulfilled life. https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/02/hout.text: The Saudi-led coalition accused Yemen's Houthis of striking a power station in the holy city of Medina in Saudi Arabia, a claim the Iran-backed group denied.The alleged attack came as fighting intensified in Yemen, where forces of the internationally recognised government said they carried out attacks on Houthi targets and witnesses heard explosions in the Houthi-held capital Sana'a.The Saudi-led coalition said on Thursday a drone struck Medina's Taibah electricity distribution station, which provides power to the Prophet's Mosque.Medina, the burial place of the Prophet Mohammed and home to the Prophet's Mosque, is one of Islam's holiest cities alongside Mecca.Coalition spokesman Major General Turki al-Maliki said a drone struck the Taibah electricity distribution station at 5:11 am (3:11 am CEST) on Tuesday."The investigation and evidence gathered by the competent authorities have confirmed the involvement of the terrorist Houthi militia in planning and executing this cowardly terrorist act, based on after-action review and the wreckage of the drone used," he said in a statement.The coalition said one transformer was taken out of service without affecting the wider electricity network. Al-Maliki said the facility supplied electricity to the Prophet's Mosque."This cowardly terrorist act, targeting a civilian facility providing electricity to the Prophet's Mosque in Medina, is a continuation of this extremist militia's attempts to target the Two Holy Mosques," he said.On Thursday, a senior Houthi official again rejected allegations that the movement had targeted Islamic holy sites, stating they were a "lie" to further back previous claims, according to Houthi-run news agency Saba.The group had firmly rejected Riyadh's accusations in mid-September of a drone attack on Mecca, Islam's holiest site."Our operations target its oil facilities and military bases, which are far removed from the sacred sites," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said at the time, adding that "fabrications and lies propagated by the criminal al-Saud regime cannot deceive anyone."Mecca is Islam's holiest site, home to the Kaaba — which Muslims worldwide turn toward for prayer — and the destination of the Hajj pilgrimage, one of the faith's Five Pillars or main tenets.The accusation came as fighting intensified in Yemen, as the internationally recognised government's military said it had carried out strikes on Houthi targets in Sana'a, Saada and Taiz.A spokesman said the military had conducted a "high-value targeting operation" in Sana'a and struck 11 targets in Saada.He added that 27 air strikes had targeted an "integrated military system" belonging to the Houthis in Taiz.The Houthis, who control Sana'a and much of Yemen's Red Sea coast, have repeatedly launched drones and missiles at Saudi Arabia since the kingdom intervened in Yemen's civil war in 2015.Any confirmed attack on either Mecca or Medina would put the perpetrators beyond the pale in the eyes of virtually the entire Muslim world, Shia and Sunni alike.Ankara blasts 'provocative attacks'Turkey strongly condemned the alleged attack and voiced support for Saudi Arabia."We strongly condemn the Houthis' attack on civilian infrastructure" in Medina, the foreign ministry said."These provocative attacks, which threaten Saudi Arabia's sovereignty and security and target the sacred values of the Islamic world, must cease immediately and unconditionally."Turkey said it reiterated its "strong support for Saudi Arabia" and called for steps to prevent further escalation.Qatar also condemned the attack. In a statement, Doha said it was "a grave assault on the sanctity of Islamic holy sites", a violation of Saudi sovereignty and international law.It reaffirmed its "full solidarity" with Riyadh and said the kingdom's security was integral to Gulf security.The League of Arab States joined the condemnation, calling the attack "an unacceptable transgression".The organisation said the attack "provokes the sentiments of Muslims worldwide" and represented a dangerous escalation.Al-Azhar, the Cairo-based institute of Sunni Islamic learning, also denounced the incident, stating that "targeting Medina provokes the sentiments of Muslims worldwide".The Houthis are Zaydi Shia Muslims, a specific branch of Islam historically rooted in northern Yemen that is theologically distinct from both the Twelver Shia Islam dominant in Iran and Saudi Arabia's Wahhabi-influenced Sunni tradition.The group formally known as Ansar Allah is tied to Tehran's so-called Axis of Resistance — a loose network of militant groups in several countries in the region including Hezbollah in Lebanon, Hamas in Gaza and militias in Iraq, all backed, trained and equipped by the IRGC to varying degrees.

https://www.dw.com/en/school-roof-collap.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OGmx Emergency services were working to clear the rubble, looking for more survivors Image: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Province's Emergency Service/AFP Advertisement Officials in Peshawar, Pakistan, confirmed on Thursday that at least 32 pupils under the age of 13 died when an elementary school roof collapsed in the Afridi Abad area of the city. One teacher has also died, they said. The deceased, along with more than 50 other injured people, were brought to Lady Reading Hospital as rescue workers rushed to clear the rubble and search for more survivors. "We have taken out ​at ‌least 45 children," said district emergency officer Iftikhar Khan, but added that more children were thought to still be under the rubble. From her hospital bed, a teacher told reporters that the school had three floors and more than 1,200 pupils and staff. The cause of the disaster was not immediately clear. Roof collapses becoming more regular Local media in Pakistan noted that such incidents are becoming increasingly routine across the country, due to poor building standards and maintenance. In July, three young girls were killed near Umerkot when the outer wall of a government school gave way. That same month, one child died and five were injured in Lahore when the roof of an under-construction private school collapsed. One month earlier, 14 children were killed in a similar manner at a private tutoring facility in Lahore, which came shortly after yet another such incident in Dera Ghazi Khan.
